“Seema, you've been staring at that page for an hour,” Uday said from the doorway.
“Bhaiya, I'm not staring, I'm working it out.” Seema tapped her pencil against her cheek, then turned the page toward him. Three columns: Say nothing. Talk to Ritu. Tell Sir.
“Who's Ritu?”
“My friend who copied in the maths test. Under Say nothing I wrote: honest kids lose marks, and she'll probably do it again.”
“And Talk to Ritu?”
“It might get awkward, but she gets a chance to stop. Under Tell Sir: she could be in real trouble and it could follow her, but the copying ends.”
Uday read it twice. “Which column is worst?”
“Silence, I think. It's the only one where nobody gets to fix anything.”
“So what's step one?”
“Talk to her. Tomorrow. And if she laughs it off, Sir.”

qa.q: What are the three columns on Seema's page?
qa.a: The three columns are Say nothing, Talk to Ritu and Tell Sir.

qa.q: How does Seema feel about staying silent?
qa.a: Seema feels uneasy about it and judges it the worst column, because nobody gets to fix anything.

qa.q: What could Seema do if Ritu laughs it off?
qa.a: Seema could tell Sir calmly and factually, since talking first gave Ritu a chance and the harm to honest classmates would continue.

qa.q: How might Ritu see Seema's plan to talk first?
qa.a: Ritu may feel embarrassed or defensive at first, but may also be relieved to get a chance to stop before a teacher hears.

passage:
Last term I spent a whole Sunday afternoon on one page of my notebook. I'm Aadhya, and I'd seen Zubin, who I've known since we were six, reading answers off his smartwatch in the physics test.
I split the page into three: stay silent, talk to Zubin, tell Mr Das.
Stay silent: easy for now. But the honest kids, the ones who studied till midnight, get pushed down the rank list. And Zubin learns that it works, which isn't good for him later, in the boards, where it won't.
Talk to Zubin: he might be angry. Things between us could get awkward. But he gets a chance to stop or own up before anyone else knows.
Tell Mr Das: fairest to the class. But it could hurt Zubin badly, a zero, maybe his parents called, and he'd know it was me.
Seeing it written down, the middle column looked strongest as a first step. So that's what I did on Monday.

qa.q: What were the three options on Aadhya's page?
qa.a: Stay silent, talk to Zubin, tell Mr Das.

qa.q: How did Aadhya feel once it was all written down?
qa.a: Aadhya felt clearer and steadier, seeing the middle column look strongest as a first step.

qa.q: What should Aadhya do if talking to Zubin doesn't work?
qa.a: Move to the third column and tell Mr Das calmly, since fairness to honest classmates still matters.

qa.q: How would staying silent affect the honest classmates?
qa.a: They would be pushed down the rank list by someone who copied, despite studying till midnight.

grounding: Shows a student writing out what follows from staying silent, talking to the friend or telling a teacher, including harm to honest classmates, the friendship and the friend's future.

Counsellor's note, Wednesday
Avni came in during the break with a folded sheet of paper and asked if she could think out loud with me. She had seen her friend Shankar copying in the English test and did not know what to do.
She had already done most of the work. The sheet had three headings: say nothing, speak to Shankar, tell the class teacher. Under each she had written what could happen. Saying nothing: the students who worked honestly lose out in ranks, and Shankar keeps skipping the learning he will need later. Speaking to him: the friendship might wobble, but he gets a chance to stop himself. Telling the teacher: fairest, but might feel like betrayal and could affect his record.
I mainly asked questions. She decided herself that she would speak to Shankar first, this week, and go to the teacher if it continued. She looked calmer when she left.

qa.q: What were the three headings on Avni's sheet?
qa.a: Say nothing, speak to Shankar, tell the class teacher.

qa.q: How did Avni seem when she left?
qa.a: Avni seemed calmer, the worry eased by having a clear first step.

qa.q: Why is writing out consequences useful in a choice like this?
qa.a: It makes the harm to classmates, the friendship and Shankar's future visible, so the decision isn't driven only by fear.

qa.q: How might Shankar's future be affected if nothing is said?
qa.a: Shankar could keep skipping the learning he'll need later, which might hurt him more in bigger exams.

grounding: A counsellor notes a student weighing silence, speaking to the friend or telling a teacher, including harm to honest classmates and the friend's future.
